name: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome
rawContent:
# Fitz-Hugh-Curtis Syndrome: Comprehensive Reference for Foundation Year Doctors

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Definition and Key Concepts
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (FHCS) is perihepatitis—inflammation of the liver capsule and surrounding peritoneum—that occurs as a complication of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). It is characterized by right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain and is most commonly associated with Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections ascending from the lower genital tract.

### Epidemiology
FHCS occurs in approximately 5-10% of women with PID, predominantly affecting sexually active women of reproductive age (15-35 years). It is often underdiagnosed due to atypical presentation. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common causative organism (>70%), followed by N. gonorrhoeae.

### Essential Pathophysiology
Ascending infection from the cervix and endometrium spreads to the fallopian tubes (salpingitis) and can extend to the peritoneal cavity. Bacteria or inflammatory mediators travel along the paracolic gutters to the right upper abdomen, causing inflammation of Glisson's capsule (liver capsule) and adjacent peritoneum. This creates characteristic "violin-string" adhesions between the liver capsule and anterior abdominal wall, visible on laparoscopy. Left-sided involvement is rare but possible.

## 2. RECOGNITION

### Key Symptoms
- Right upper quadrant pain (hallmark feature—pleuritic, sharp, may mimic cholecystitis)
- Lower abdominal/pelvic pain (concurrent PID symptoms)
- Abnormal vaginal discharge
- Fever (may be absent in mild cases)
- Dyspareunia
- Intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding
- Pain worse on movement or deep breathing

### Key Signs
- RUQ tenderness (often disproportionate to examination findings)
- Cervical motion tenderness ("chandelier sign")
- Adnexal tenderness
- Pelvic tenderness on bimanual examination
- Fever (>38°C in ~50% of cases)
- Peritoneal signs may be present
- Hepatomegaly absent (liver function typically normal)

### Atypical Presentations
- Isolated RUQ pain without pelvic symptoms (10-15% of cases)
- Predominantly respiratory symptoms (pleuritic chest pain, shoulder tip pain)
- Chronic presentation with recurrent RUQ pain
- Minimal or absent fever
- Asymptomatic PID with incidental finding on imaging

### Red Flags Requiring Immediate Action
- Signs of sepsis (tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental state)
- Peritonitis (rebound tenderness, guarding, rigidity)
- Severe RUQ pain with vomiting suggesting biliary pathology
- Pregnancy-positive test (ectopic pregnancy must be excluded)
- Signs of tubo-ovarian abscess (pelvic mass, severe pain)

## 3. INVESTIGATION

### First-line Investigations
- Pregnancy test (urine β-hCG)—mandatory in all women of childbearing age
- Cervical/vaginal swabs for Chlamydia (NAAT) and Gonorrhea (NAAT)
- High vaginal swab for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity
- Full blood count (raised WCC, neutrophilia)
- CRP/ESR (elevated inflammatory markers)
- Liver function tests (typically normal; mild transaminase elevation in 25%)
- Urinalysis (exclude UTI/pyelonephritis)

### Second-line Investigations
- Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal preferred)—assess for tubo-ovarian abscess, free fluid, hydrosalpinx
- Abdominal ultrasound—exclude gallbladder pathology (cholecystitis, cholelithiasis)
- HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B/C serology (STI screen)
- Blood cultures if febrile

### Specialist Tests
- Laparoscopy (gold standard for diagnosis)—direct visualization of "violin-string" adhesions between liver and abdominal wall, pelvic inflammation
- CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast—if diagnosis uncertain or complications suspected
- MRI pelvis—for complex cases or when ultrasound non-diagnostic
- Endometrial biopsy (histology showing endometritis)

## 4. DIAGNOSIS

### Diagnostic Criteria or Clinical Decision Rules
Diagnosis is primarily clinical:
- RUQ pain in a sexually active woman PLUS
- Evidence of PID (cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, abnormal discharge) PLUS
- Positive STI testing (Chlamydia/Gonorrhea) or elevated inflammatory markers
- In the absence of other causes of RUQ pain

Definitive diagnosis requires laparoscopy showing perihepatitis and characteristic adhesions, but this is reserved for atypical/severe cases.

### Key Differential Diagnoses to Exclude
- Acute cholecystitis/cholelithiasis (fever, Murphy's sign, gallbladder wall thickening on USS)
- Hepatitis (jaundice, significantly elevated transaminases)
- Acute pancreatitis (elevated amylase/lipase, epigastric pain radiating to back)
- Appendicitis (RIF > RUQ pain, McBurney's point tenderness)
- Pneumonia (lower lobe—pleuritic pain, respiratory symptoms, CXR changes)
- Pulmonary embolism (pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, risk factors)
- Pyelonephritis (flank pain, urinary symptoms, positive urine culture)
- Ectopic pregnancy (positive pregnancy test, adnexal mass)
- Perforated peptic ulcer (sudden severe pain, peritonism, free air on imaging)
- Subphrenic abscess (post-surgical, persistent fever)

## 5. MANAGEMENT

### Acute Management (Emergency/Immediate Care)

#### First-line Treatments
- **Empirical antibiotics for PID** (start immediately—do not delay for test results):
  - **Outpatient regimen**: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose PLUS Doxycycline 100 mg BD PO for 14 days PLUS Metronidazole 400 mg BD PO for 14 days
  - **Alternative**: Ofloxacin 400 mg BD PLUS Metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days (if ceftriaxone unavailable/penicillin allergy; avoid if gonorrhea suspected due to resistance)
- **Analgesia**: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 400 mg TDS) or paracetamol 1g QDS
- **Contact tracing and partner notification**: Refer to sexual health clinic
- **Advise sexual abstinence** until completion of treatment and partner treated

#### Second-line Treatments
- **Inpatient IV antibiotics** if:
  - Severe symptoms, vomiting, unable to tolerate oral
  - Pregnancy
  - Tubo-ovarian abscess suspected
  - Failed outpatient treatment
  - Diagnostic uncertainty
  - Immunocompromised
- **IV regimen**: Ceftriaxone 2g IV OD PLUS Doxycycline 100 mg BD PO (or IV if vomiting) PLUS Metronidazole 500 mg IV TDS
- Switch to oral when afebrile for 24h and clinically improving (complete 14 days total)

#### Emergency Procedures
- **Laparoscopy**: For diagnostic uncertainty, failed medical management, suspected abscess requiring drainage, or severe peritonitis
- **Laparotomy**: For ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess or generalized peritonitis not responding to conservative management

### Chronic Management (Ongoing Care)

#### First-line Treatments
- **Complete 14-day antibiotic course** (compliance crucial)
- **Partner treatment**: All sexual partners within 6 months should be tested and treated empirically
- **Test of cure**: Repeat NAAT for Chlamydia/Gonorrhea 3-6 weeks post-treatment (not earlier due to false positives from dead organisms)
- **Contraceptive advice**: Consider long-acting reversible contraception (LARC)
- **STI prevention counseling**: Barrier contraception, regular screening

#### Second-line Treatments
- **Gynecology follow-up** if:
  - Persistent symptoms post-treatment
  - Recurrent PID
  - Fertility concerns (refer for tubal assessment)
  - Chronic pelvic pain

#### Monitoring Requirements
- Clinical review at 3 days (in-person or phone) to ensure improving
- Test of cure at 3-6 weeks post-treatment
- Annual STI screening if risk factors persist
- Fertility counseling if planning pregnancy (increased ectopic risk)

## 6. DRUGS & PROCEDURES

### Drugs

#### Ceftriaxone
- **Mechanism of Action**: Third-generation cephalosporin—inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis; broad-spectrum activity including Neisseria gonorrhoeae
- **Typical Dosing Range**: 500 mg IM single dose (outpatient); 2 g IV OD (inpatient)
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: Hypersensitivity reactions, diarrhea, injection site pain; avoid in severe penicillin allergy (10% cross-reactivity)
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: First-line for gonorrhea; use alternative if severe beta-lactam allergy

#### Doxycycline
- **Mechanism of Action**: Tetracycline antibiotic—inhibits bacterial protein synthesis; excellent activity against Chlamydia trachomatis and Mycoplasma genitalium
- **Typical Dosing Range**: 100 mg BD for 14 days
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: Photosensitivity, esophagitis (take with food, remain upright 30 min), nausea; contraindicated in pregnancy and children <12 years; avoid in renal impairment
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: First-line for Chlamydia PID; use azithromycin in pregnancy (1 g weekly × 2 weeks) or erythromycin

#### Metronidazole
- **Mechanism of Action**: Nitroimidazole antibiotic with anaerobic and protozoal activity; disrupts DNA
- **Typical Dosing Range**: 400-500 mg BD-TDS for 14 days
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: Metallic taste, nausea, disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (strict alcohol avoidance); peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: Covers anaerobes (Bacteroides spp.) common in PID; essential component of PID regimen

### Procedures

#### Laparoscopy
- **What it Involves**: Minimally invasive surgery under general anesthesia; camera inserted through umbilicus to visualize pelvis and upper abdomen; therapeutic (adhesiolysis, abscess drainage) or diagnostic
- **Indications**: Diagnostic uncertainty, failed medical management, suspected tubo-ovarian abscess, severe peritonitis, atypical presentation
- **Key Risks/Complications**: Infection, bleeding, bowel/bladder/vascular injury (<1%), conversion to laparotomy, anesthetic risks, venous thromboembolism

## 7. PROGNOSIS & COMPLICATIONS

### Expected Outcomes
With prompt antibiotic treatment, most women recover fully within 2-3 weeks. However, 10-20% develop long-term sequelae. Delayed treatment significantly increases complication risk.

### Important Complications to Watch For
- **Infertility**: 10-15% after single PID episode; risk increases with recurrent episodes (up to 50% after 3 episodes)
- **Chronic pelvic pain**: 20-30% develop chronic pain due to adhesions
- **Ectopic pregnancy**: 6-10-fold increased risk due to tubal damage
- **Tubo-ovarian abscess**: 15-20% of PID cases; requires IV antibiotics ± drainage
- **Peritonitis**: Rare but life-threatening
- **Recurrent PID**: 20-25% recurrence rate (often reinfection)
- **Perihepatitis adhesions**: May cause chronic RUQ pain, though usually resolve with treatment
- **Fertility issues**: Refer for early fertility assessment if attempting to conceive

## 8. FOUNDATION DOCTOR ROLE

### Specific Responsibilities and Limitations
Foundation doctors should:
- Recognize the classical presentation (RUQ pain + PID symptoms in sexually active woman)
- Exclude pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy urgently
- Initiate first-line investigations (pregnancy test, STI swabs, FBC, CRP, LFTs)
- Start empirical antibiotics promptly (do not delay for swab results)
- Arrange appropriate imaging (pelvic USS, consider abdominal USS)
- Provide sexual health counseling and arrange partner notification
- Know when to escalate (see below)

### When to Escalate to Senior/Specialist
- **Immediate escalation** (same-day senior/gynecology review):
  - Pregnancy-positive (potential ectopic)
  - Signs of sepsis or peritonitis
  - Severe pain with vomiting
  - Pelvic mass on examination (possible abscess)
  - Diagnostic uncertainty
- **Urgent escalation** (within 24-48 hours):
  - Not responding to oral antibiotics after 3 days
  - Unable to tolerate oral medications
  - Immunocompromised patient
- **Routine referral**:
  - Recurrent PID
  - Fertility concerns
  - Chronic pelvic pain post-treatment

### Key Safety Considerations
- **Always exclude pregnancy** before diagnosing FHCS—ectopic pregnancy can present with RUQ pain and mimic this condition
- **Do not delay antibiotics** waiting for test results—treat empirically based on clinical suspicion
- **Partner notification is mandatory**—untreated partners lead to reinfection
- **Document clearly**: Sexual history, examination findings, antibiotic allergies, partner notification plan
- **Safeguarding**: Consider sexual exploitation/abuse in vulnerable patients (adolescents, learning disabilities)
- **Follow-up essential**: Ensure test of cure arranged and patient understands long-term risks (ectopic pregnancy, infertility)
